newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Russian troops under fire on Tajik-Afghan border.
newsitem.headline: Russian troops under fire on Tajik-Afghan border.

text.p: Russian troops guarding Tajikistan's border with Afghanistan took no chances on Tuesday despite a planned accord aimed at ending a four-year civil war in the ex-Soviet state.

Tajikistan's secular government and its Islamist opposition foes are set to sign a peace agreement on June 27 in Moscow, but the border guards said they had been attacked only last week by Tajik opposition forces based in Afghanistan.

A few hundred metres (yards) back from Pyandzh River, which marks the country's frontier with Afghanistan, soldiers with Russia's Federal Border Service, rifles poking out of stone culverts, carefully scanned the passes inside Afghan territory.
"We came under fire on June 10," Lieutenant Piotr Raichinets told a group of reporters taken by the Russian military to visit the remote post set in the green foothills of the rugged Pamir mountains.

Russian troops said the attack came from an 80-strong group loyal to Tajikistan's Islamist opposition trying to cross the treacherous river from a camp inside lawless Afghanistan. The Tajik opposition denounced the allegations as a "provocation" by the Russian military.
"I gave the order to open return fire and we fought for 40 minutes," said the officer, wearing a tan summer uniform.
He showed reporters a van shredded by machine-gun bullets by way of testimony to the fire-fight.
"We killed about 20 of their number but it was hard to tell as the Pyandzh swept a lot of the bodies away," he said.
Skirmishes on the Tajik-Afghan frontier, with drug traffickers as well as guerrillas operating out of Afghanistan, have occurred with monotonous regularity.

But last week's reported fighting rattled nerves after months of careful negotiations in the lead up to next week's signing and showed an underlying fragility to the truce declared between government and guerrillas last December.
Tens of thousands of the 5.7 million population were killed in the civil war and many more were driven from their homes.
An old armoured personnel carrier was dug in as part of Dzhavai's defences. There was no movement on the opposite bank.
In some of the dugouts, soldiers, including those from the Central Asian state of Kazakhstan serving as peacekeepers, breakfasted on sausages and buckwheat porridge washed down with hot, sweet tea.
Other members of the unit had left for nearby Kalaikhumb for their weekly bath.
A decade ago, Russian soldiers were deployed on the other side of the border during the Soviet Union's costly and disastrous invasion of Afghanistan.
Russia now deploys about 20,000 troops in Tajikistan, a self-proclaimed buttress against the encroachment of radical Islam inside its former Central Asian colonies.

Tensions were heightened last month after Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban militia swept north towards the borders of former Soviet Central Asia before being repulsed by ousted Afghan government forces.

Davlat Makhmad, commander of the 976th battalion of Afghan border troops, loyal to the ousted government, was in Kalaikhumb on Tuesday to discuss the situation on the frontier with his Russian counterparts.
"It is the local people who suffer in these attacks," he said, saying an Afghan woman had been killed by a stray bullet in last week's fire-fight.

The Russians, too, have suffered losses in Tajikistan, but mostly in guerrilla attacks on personnel in the capital, Dushanbe. Interfax news agency reported that a Russian army major had been shot and killed on a city street on Tuesday.
